Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:126: Nevertheless, the most agreed-upon correction for the conjugal timing of Torah scholars is from Sabbath to Sabbath, and it is likewise said in Tikkunim (21a): further, this whole "tree" is Tzadik, which is "a fruit tree bearing fruit after its kind" (Genesis 1:11), and this is the day of Shabbat, for there is the union of the Shechinah with the Holy One, blessed be He, and there she has rest; of this it is said (Psalms 1:3), "and he shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, whose fruit he gives in its season" — this is the "season" of Tzadik, which is Friday night, from which new souls blossom in Israel on Friday evening, called "new faces." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:127: Further, in Tikkunim (90a), he expounds there regarding forbidden relations, and says afterward: and although all these forbidden relations are said of the sefirot and the Name YHVH, this is not [true] in its place above; rather, when the Shechinah is exiled, all the sefirot descend with her, and there is no separation between her and the ten sefirot, and when they descend they clothe themselves in the six weekdays, six branches, etc. And he says afterward: and why is there separation? Because there is no Tzadik, this being the sign of the covenant, there [i.e., in exile] — and the secret of the matter is "there is no righteous man [tzadik] in the land" [meaning] that the sign of the covenant is there [absent, unavailable]. But on Shabbat, which is the seventh day, there is closeness and unification of the Name YHVH and all the sefirot; therefore Torah scholars have their union from Friday night to Friday night, for these are certainly forbidden relations below, but above it is said (Psalms 5:5), "evil shall not sojourn with You." And a Tzadik who approaches his wife on weekdays — that son he begets, of him it is said, "a righteous man to whom evil happens," for he causes the holy to become weekday, that is, the seventh day, and at that time it is the secret of "a righteous man to whom evil happens"; but above there is no forbidden relation, no severance, and no separation. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:128: What is meant by "he causes the holy to become weekday" is explained as follows: the attribute of Tzadik is called "the seventh day," as is likewise explained in Tikkunim (84a): but the dominion of Tzadik is the seventh day, in which all the sefirot are called "sevenths." The reason is explained in Tikkunim, Tikkun 30, at the beginning of the Tikkun (73b); see there, for its secret is the secret of the letter zayin [7], which is in Tzadik, namely yod upon vav, a crown upon its head; and since it is seventh it is holy, as explained in Tikkun 47 (84a), and one should not draw it into the weekday, so as not to mix holy with weekday. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:129: Likewise, the correction of the sign of the covenant is to reveal secrets to one who is righteous and God-fearing, as it is written (Psalms 25:14), "the secret of the LORD is for those who fear Him." And so it says in Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash, 2a), found among us in manuscript: and whoever reveals secrets to the righteous causes the Tzadik to shine with the secrets of Torah and the Shechinah, for "raz" [secret] is called "or" [light], and at that time (Daniel 12:3), "and those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:130: Also, the student should correct his soul through occupation with Torah by way of secret [Kabbalah], as explained in Tikkunim, Tikkun 30 (73b), regarding the punishment of those who withhold themselves from reading the wisdom of Kabbalah. These are his words, in brief: these make the Torah dry and do not wish to occupy themselves with the wisdom of Kabbalah, causing the flowing spring, which is the yod, to be removed from it, leaving the bet [i.e., 'the Torah'] dry — woe to them, for they cause poverty, sword, plunder, killing, and destruction in the world. Thus far his words; the rest of his words we copied in the introduction.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:131: And one who reveals secrets of the Torah to one who is unworthy, besides his punishment in the World to Come, also has his punishment in this world, that poverty pursues him; and so it says in the Zohar (beginning of portion Vayikra, 2b): this letter [aleph] stands for the punishment of one who reveals secrets, and your sign is "reish" and "kalon" [poverty and shame]. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:132: Likewise, in the Ra'aya Meheimna (portion Pinchas, 244a), regarding what is written there, that one who throws crumbs on the ground is pursued by poverty, the Faithful Shepherd says: whoever disgraces the crumbs of bread and throws them in a place where it is not needed — all the more so one who disgraces the drops of brain-matter, that is, of seed, and throws them on the ground, of whom it is said (Genesis 6:12), "for all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth," or throws them into a niddah, or the daughter of a foreign god, or a maidservant, or a harlot — all the more so, and all the more so, one who disgraces the crumbs of Torah, which are the thorns of letters and the crowns of letters, of which it is said, whoever makes improper use of the crown perishes — all the more so one who hands over the secrets of Torah and the secrets of Kabbalah and the secrets of the account of creation, or the secrets of the letters of the Ineffable Name, to people who are not fit, over whom the evil inclination rules — a harlot woman, of whom it is said (Proverbs 6:26), "for on account of a harlot woman, a man is reduced to a loaf of bread" — and there is no "bread" but Torah, and there is no "loaf" but a single halakhah. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:133: And in the Ra'aya Meheimna (portion Ekev, 272a) it explains that just as poverty pursues him regarding sustenance, so poverty pursues him from attaining Torah. These are his words: and the ten vowel-points of the holy Name are called crumbs the size of an olive, and these correspond to the drops of seed; and whoever disgraces them and throws them in a place where it is not needed, poverty pursues him and he goes wandering and fleeing — this is what is written (Job 15:23), "he wanders about for bread, saying, where?" — and there is no "bread" but Torah, and he cries out "where is" one who has mercy on him, that he not be forgotten; and the crumbs the size of an olive are in Tzadik, who is pressed, pressed like olives. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:134: Also among the qualities that merit the attribute of Tzadik: one who rises early to be first in the synagogue stands at the level of Tzadik. This is likewise explained in the Zohar (portion Terumah, 131a), these are his words: and whoever comes early attaches himself to the Shechinah in a single attachment. Come and see, that first one found in the synagogue and who tarries in the synagogue — fortunate is his portion, for he stands at the level of Tzadik together with the Shechinah, and this is (Proverbs 8:17), "and those who seek Me early [meshacharai] shall find Me" — this one rises with a supernal ascent. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:135: Further, one who merits the attribute of Tzadik is one who gives charity, and this is explained in Tikkunim as a correction for the sign of the covenant; and likewise to fulfill the mitzvah of oneg Shabbat [the delight of Shabbat]. These are the words of Tikkunim (58a): further, the Shechinah is called Tzedakah [charity], and the Holy One, blessed be He, is the Master of Charity; in exile she is poor and her children are poor, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is as it were poor when He is out of His place, and of this it is said (Isaiah 33:7), "behold, their valiant ones cry out outside." And in what place is He poor and she poor? In Tzadik, which is the covenant — for because Israel sinned against it below, this river shall dry up and become desolate in the First and Second Temples, and the Shechinah is desolate and dry through it; and because they cause the waters to be gathered from it, the Shechinah remains dry — this is what is written (Genesis 1:9), "let the waters be gathered to one place, and let the dry land appear." And whoever gives charity to the poor causes that river drawn from Eden, which is the supernal Mother, to water the garden, which is a "door" (dalet), poor (dalah). And the day of Shabbat is poor, and whoever fulfills the delight of Shabbat causes that door to be watered, and that poor one becomes filled and is called a river; and whoever has the ability to fulfill the delight of Shabbat and does not do so — the delight is turned for him into the affliction of tzara'at, and his house and his money are laid waste. Thus far his words. And likewise regarding this punishment, he speaks at the end of 18.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:136: Further, in Tikkun 24 (69b), regarding the delight of Shabbat: one must fulfill in it the delight [oneg], which is Tzadik, that issues from Eden, which is Binah, the World to Come, to water — this is the lower Shechinah — and the river is the vav that issues from Yod-Heh and travels five hundred years, which are the five sefirot, and reaches Tzadik to water from it the garden, which is heh; therefore "a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife" (Genesis 2:24). Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:137: Further, regarding charity meriting the level of Tzadik, it is explained in the Zohar (portion Behar Sinai, 110b), these are his words, on "and if you say, what shall we eat" (Leviticus 25:20): Rabbi Yehuda opened (Psalms 37:3), "trust in the LORD and do good; dwell in the land and cultivate faith" — a person should always be watchful with his Master and attach his heart to supernal faith, in order to be whole with his Master, for when he is whole with Him, none of the people of the world can harm him. Come and see: "trust in the LORD and do good" — rather, we have learned thus: through an act below, an act is aroused above, and they have established, "and you shall do them" — as though you will make them, for it is your arousal that you do below, and it arouses above. Therefore it is written, "and do good," and "good" is nothing but Tzadik, as it is written (Isaiah 3:10), "say of the righteous [tzadik] that it is good" — since you do [good], certainly this "good" is aroused, then "dwell in the land and cultivate faith," and it is all one. "Dwell in the land" — the supernal land, for you cannot dwell with her until this "good" is aroused toward her; once it is aroused, it is as though he himself made it, and then "dwell in the land" — dwell within her, eat her fruit, enjoy yourself with her, and "cultivate faith" — this is the land, and it is all one, as in (Psalms 92:3), "and Your faithfulness in the nights" — "cultivate faith" means, remember her in all your desires. And if you do not arouse this "good" toward her, you become distant from her and cannot approach her — do not approach into a burning fire; and if you approach her, [do so] with fear, like one who fears death, for then the fire is blazing and burns the world with its flames. But once you arouse this "good" toward her, then (Job 22:28), "you shall decree a thing and it shall be established for you, and light shall shine on your ways."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:138: Come and see: the people of faith speak this intent every day. Who are the people of faith? Those who arouse this "good" toward it, and do not spare their own [possessions], knowing that the Holy One, blessed be He, gives him more, as in (Proverbs 11:24), "there is one who scatters, yet increases more." Why? Because this arouses blessings toward him, and he should not say, "if I give this now, what will I do tomorrow?" Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, gives him blessings without limit, as they have established. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:139: When the reader considers this statement, he will find that charity is a correction for the blemish of the sign of the covenant — the matter being that just as through the sin of the blemish the acts of kindness depart from Tzadik, who encompasses the five kindnesses, as explained in the Idra (142a), and it becomes a river that shall dry up and become desolate — and therefore is called "good" — so through charity one draws the kindnesses to sweeten the judgments, and this is a complete unification, as explained in the statement.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:140: This is further explained in the Zohar (portion Bechukotai, 113b), these are his words: Rabbi Shimon wept and said, woe to people who do not know and do not pay attention to the honor of their Master — who makes the Name every day? Say: whoever gives charity to the poor. And at the end of his words: fortunate is the portion of whoever merits to make the holy Name above; therefore charity ascends above all else — and this applies to charity given for its own sake, since charity arouses Tzedek to Tzadik, to join us together as one, so that the whole becomes the holy Name properly, for Tzedek is not corrected and completed except through charity, as it is written (Isaiah 54:14), "in righteousness [tzedakah] shall you be established" — and this is said of the Community of Israel; therefore, "and you shall do them" etc. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:141: Especially if he merits to be a collector of charity, he stands at the level of Tzadik and receives reward corresponding to all — and this is explained in the Zohar (portion Vayigash, 208a) on the verse (Psalms 112:9), "he has scattered, he has given to the poor." These are his words: therefore, "he has scattered, he has given to the poor" — this is Tzadik; "his righteousness [tzidkato] endures forever" — this is the Community of Israel, for through this she stands in the secret of peace [shalem], in complete establishment; "the wicked shall see it and be angered" — this refers to the kingdom of the idol-worshippers. Come and see: the kingdom of heaven is the Temple, to sustain all the poor within the shade of the Shechinah, and Tzadik is called the "collector of charity," to have compassion on and sustain all, as it is written, "he has scattered, he has given to the poor." Therefore collectors of charity receive reward corresponding to all. Thus far his words. And the whole discourse on charity that we have copied above is explained there; we have not copied his words in full, to avoid excessive length.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:142: Also, he should intend every day to make himself righteous [tzadik], and give spiritual charity, as is written in Tikkunim (33a), these are his words: and these who give You a gift with the right hand, which is Tzeda[ka]h — tzadi is ninety amens, dalet is the four holy [things], kof is a hundred blessings, heh is the five books of the Torah. Thus far his words. And elsewhere he explains that from "Tzadik" one derives the ten holy [praises] one must respond to every day.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:143: Also, one who merits the attribute of Tzadik is one who loves peace and pursues peace, since it is known that the attribute of Tzadik is called "peace" (Zohar, portion Tzav, 33a); and just as he separated peace [by his sin], so he should seek to reconcile peace between a man and his wife and between one person and another. This is likewise explained in the verses of King David, peace be upon him (Psalms 34:13-15): "who is the man who desires life, who loves days to see good?" and he says, "turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it." The aspect of "loving days to see good" is a correction for the attribute of Tzadik, and correspondingly he says "turn away from evil, seek peace and pursue it" — this refers to one called an emitter of seed in vain — and "do good" — he corrects the attribute of good through charity, as explained above; and likewise to juxtapose redemption to prayer, as is explained (Berachot 10b), "and I have done what is good in Your eyes" (Isaiah 38:3) — that he juxtaposed redemption to prayer. And the intent of "do good" is the correction of the attribute of good, called Tzadik, for the secret of unification, and therefore he must also seek peace, as explained — this aspect being the positive commandment. And the aspect of "turn away from evil," pertaining to the blemish of Tzadik, is the guarding of the tongue from every matter that blemishes it, as explained above (in this chapter and in ch. 11) regarding "guard your tongue from evil" — for one who blemishes his tongue is defiled thereby, and there is no need to elaborate further on this.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:144: Included in the correction of the attribute of peace is that one hear his own disgrace and not respond, since the attribute of peace is his accuser, he should accept the judgment of Heaven with a pleasant countenance. David, because he sinned in the matter of Bathsheba, accepted his punishment when Shimi ben Gera disgraced him, and he said (2 Samuel 16:10), "the LORD has told him to curse," and remained silent.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:145: Also, for the correction of the sign of the covenant, he should keep his eyes lowered, since through the sight of the eye the covenant becomes blemished, as it is written (Numbers 15:39), "and do not go astray after your heart and after your eyes" — heart and eye are two agents of transgression (Yerushalmi Berachot 1:5). And when the eye is blemished it is called an "evil eye," as it says (Proverbs 23:6), "do not eat the bread of one with an evil eye" — the reason being that just as the blemish of the covenant is called "evil," so the blemish in the house of the eye, which is a yod, is called "evil," since he emits the holy sight in vain, toward a place of nakedness and the like. And since we find that the correction of the covenant is "turn away from evil," this includes not having an evil eye — this being "turn away from evil" without qualification, every aspect of "evil," whether in the eye, or in the tongue as it says "guard your tongue from evil," or in the covenant — for in all of these the term "evil" applies, as we have elaborated.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:146: One who guards his sight is bound to Chesed, since the lion is to the right, as explained several times in Tikkunim (122a), and your sign is (Ezekiel 1:10), "and the face of the lion was to the right" — and "lion" [aryeh] is [related to] "sight" [re'iyah]. And Abraham our father, peace be upon him, because his intent was always to be bound to the right, said (Genesis 12:11), "behold now, I know" etc., and our Sages of blessed memory explained (Tanchuma, Lech Lecha 5) that he saw her reflection in the water. And all the aspects of the corrections of the eyes explained above are all corrections for the sign of the covenant, since Joseph holds onto the eyes, as it is written (Genesis 49:22), "Joseph is a fruitful bough, a fruitful bough by a spring [ayin, also 'eye']" — and Joseph also holds onto the aspect of the dissection of the eye, as explained in its place (Gate of Holiness, ch. 8). Especially since seed is [related to] the light of a person's eyes (Rambam, De'ot 4:19), and once he blemishes the seed, a tear descends from his eyes, and the tear diminishes the seed, as explained in tractate Gittin (70a), since the tear is also from the light of the eyes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:147: Also pertaining to the correction of the attribute of Tzadik is to be pious [chasid], and to be careful in all the qualities explained in the Gate of Love (ch. 11) that constitute what is called "pious," the reason being that the attribute of Tzadik is called Chesed, as is likewise explained in the Idra (portion Naso, 142a), these are his words: and this "amah" [forearm/cubit] is called Chesed, and likewise at the end of Idra Ha'azinu (296a-b); and since he has blemished Chesed, it is fitting that he grasp all the qualities of Chesed, as explained there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:148: Fortunate is one who can fulfill the mortification that Rabbi Yishmael performed, as explained in Pirkei Heichalot, which we copied in the Gate of Repentance, chapter 5. For in doing these things, one departs from the powers of judgment and Gevurah and attaches himself to Chesed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:149: One who merits the attribute of Tzadik merits having the Shechinah rest upon him, since when the covenant is blemished, the blemish touches upon her — for the covenant encompasses circumcision and peri'ah [uncovering], which are Tzadik and Tzadik, as explained in portion Emor (91b). And after the correction of the covenant, this is a preparation to merit the land of the living, as it is said (Psalms 37:29), "the righteous shall inherit the land."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:150: Likewise it says further in the Zohar (portion Shelach Lecha, 160a), regarding the counsels of the evil inclination, discussing the refutation of its counsels: what do the people of faith say? "If the LORD delights in us, He will give it to us" — since when a person strives with the desire of his heart toward the Holy One, blessed be He, He asks of us only the heart, and they should guard that holy sign, as it is said (Isaiah 60:21), "and your people, all of them righteous, shall inherit the land forever." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:151: Also I have heard, regarding the correction of the sign of the covenant, that one should strive to bring people back in repentance, corresponding to the blemish of emitting seed outward — for every drop of seed is a soul seized in the hand of the external force. Therefore, correspondingly, he should strive to bring out people who are handed over to the external force and bring them within, into holiness, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 51:15), "I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners shall return to You." And it is known that Tzadik is called "a tongue of teachings [limudim]," as explained in portion Pinchas (250a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:152: All these are particular aspects pertaining to the attribute of Tzadik. But one must also correct all the aspects of the attributes for the whole Shiur Komah, since the blemish of the covenant touches the whole Shiur Komah, for the covenant encompasses YHVH, which is the totality of the whole Shiur Komah, as explained above. Therefore Rashbi, peace be upon him, said (Zohar, portion Vayakhel, 214b), which we copied above, regarding the blemish of the covenant, "these words apply when he has not done complete repentance, repentance sufficient to cover all his deeds." And at the end of his words: because there is no sin as harsh before the Holy One, blessed be He, as one who deals falsely with and blemishes this holy marked sign — of this sin it is written (Genesis 38:10), "and what he did was evil in the eyes of the LORD." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:153: The reason has already been explained above, that the Name YHVH is sealed in the covenant, as is written in Tikkunim (65), "*Mi *ya'aleh *lanu *hashamaymah," whose initial letters spell Milah [circumcision] and final letters spell YHVH; and just as the Name YHVH is the root of all Names, as is known, so the covenant is the essential support that maintains the whole body, and one who blemishes it is as though he blemishes YHVH itself, which encompasses all the attributes. Therefore he needs repentance "sufficient to cover all his deeds" — meaning, as though he had blemished all his organs, and all his deeds are blemished; and through this repentance he corrects everything.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:154: How is this done? He must perform mitzvot with all his organs. And so Rabbeinu Yonah, peace be upon him, wrote in Sha'arei Teshuvah (Gate 1), these are his words: tenth, to make his deeds good in the matter in which he was arrogant: if he gazed at forbidden relations, he should conduct himself with lowered eyes; if he sinned with evil speech, he should occupy himself with Torah; and in all the organs with which he sinned, he should strive to fulfill the commandments through them, and so our Sages of blessed memory said (Shemot Rabbah 23:3), the righteous are appeased through the very thing by which they sin; further they said (Vayikra Rabbah 21:4), if you have done bundle upon bundle of transgressions, do correspondingly bundle upon bundle of mitzvot — feet that hasten to run to evil, let them run to a matter of mitzvah; a lying tongue, let his palate speak truth, let his mouth open in wisdom, and the Torah of kindness be on his tongue; hands that shed blood, let him open his hand wide to his poor; haughty eyes, let him be humble and lower his eyes; a heart that devises wicked plans, let him treasure the words of Torah in his heart and let the meditation of his heart be understanding; one who spreads discord between brothers, let him seek peace and pursue it. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:155: Likewise, our Sages of blessed memory explained the verse (Ecclesiastes 7:19), "wisdom strengthens the wise more than ten rulers," and other statements on this matter we have copied in this Gate, chapter 5; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:156: Along these lines, he must be merciful and humble, corresponding to the first [ruler/quality]; be wise, corresponding to the second; purify his thoughts and be understanding and a penitent, corresponding to the third attribute; be a doer of kindness, corresponding to the fourth attribute; be mighty in conquering his inclination, corresponding to the fifth attribute; be a master of Torah for its own sake, as explained regarding rising at midnight, corresponding to the sixth attribute; be among those who support students of Torah, corresponding to the seventh and eighth attributes; guard the covenant properly as explained, corresponding to the ninth attribute; intend in the covering of tzitzit, corresponding to the tenth attribute. And likewise the existence of the mitzvah [of tzitzit and its meaning] serves for its corrections, especially if he accepts sufferings upon himself with the intent of purifying himself from the kelipot into which he fell through his blemish; and likewise that he fix set times for Torah, corresponding to her "conjugal time," she being the King's daughter — and there are several further particulars pertaining to the correction of the tenth attribute, some of which we have already explained in the Gate of Love.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:157: One who merits to purify the attribute of the covenant with all these conditions will merit that his thoughts be pure and merit attachment to YHVH. The reason is that the supernal yod, which is in the secret of Chochmah, depends on the lower yod — this being the secret of the two yods in the aleph, and likewise the two yods in the two Names YHVH and Adonai, as explained in Tikkunim; and since the lower one is blemished, the upper one is also blemished, and while a person has not done repentance to purify the blemished attribute of the covenant, it is impossible for his thoughts to be pure enough to be attached to YHVH while standing in prayer. But one who purifies his covenant thereby purifies, as it were, the YHVH within him, and merits attachment to Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:158: This is likewise explained in the Zohar (portion Lech Lecha, 94a), that regarding the attribute of the covenant it is said (Deuteronomy 4:4), "and you who cling to YHVH your God" — and everything depends on this sign; therefore it is written (Job 19:26), "and from my flesh I shall behold God" — this is the completeness of everything, "from my flesh" literally, from this very sign. Therefore fortunate is Israel, who holds onto Him, the Holy One, blessed be He — fortunate are they in this world and in the World to Come; of them it is written, "and you who cling to YHVH," etc., "you are all alive today."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:159: Likewise, in the Zohar (portion Vayikra, 14b), these are his words: but Israel, holy ones, children of holy ones, of stock and root, are sweetened with complete, holy faith at the time they are circumcised, [holiness] rests upon everything, as it is written (Deuteronomy 4:4), "and you who cling to YHVH your God, you are all alive today." Thus far his words. May the Name grant us the merit to be among those who keep His covenant and His commandments, so that we be attached to Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 17:160: With this the chapter concludes, and this gate concludes:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:1: In explaining the word "anavah" [humility] and its virtues: the word "anavah" is derived from the language of "ani" [poor/afflicted] and "inui" [affliction], the intent being submission — for the word "ani" means submissive, and likewise (Exodus 10:3), "how long will you refuse to submit [le'anot] before Me" is translated as "to be submissive." Likewise "inui" and "ta'anit" [fasting] similarly, as it says (1 Kings 2:26), "and because you were afflicted [hitanita] in all that my father was afflicted," and many similar cases — in all of them the intent is the matter of submission.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:2: Now, the matter of submission and humility is found in the Creator, blessed be He — for although He is exalted above all the exalted and prouder than all the proud, as the verse says (Psalms 93:1), "the LORD reigns, He is clothed in majesty," humility is nevertheless attributed to Him, as King David, peace be upon him, said (ibid. 18:36), "and Your humility [anvatecha] has made me great." And it is explained in Midrash Tanchuma (Yalkut Shemuel §161) on this verse: they said, "and Your right hand has supported me" — this is Torah, "from His right hand a fiery law for them" (Deuteronomy 33:2). "And Your humility has made me great" — is there anyone more humble than the Holy One, blessed be He? A person says to his fellow, "come and adorn brides, visit the sick, bury the dead, comfort mourners," and he says to him, "I am great and rich and I am leaving" — but the Holy One, blessed be He, "and He built the rib" (Genesis 2:22), "and the LORD appeared to him" (ibid. 18:1), "and He buried him in the valley" (Deuteronomy 34:6), "and God appeared to Jacob" (Genesis 35:9).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:3: Rabbi Abba bar Acha said, the student sits to learn before his teacher, and when he finishes, the student says to the teacher, "I have wearied you." But Israel used to learn from the Holy One, blessed be He, and when they departed, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, "I have wearied you greatly," as it is said (Deuteronomy 1:6), "the LORD our God spoke to us at Horeb, saying" etc. — hence, "and Your humility has made me great."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:4: Rabbi Shimon the Nazirite says, the student says to the teacher, "come, teach me one chapter," and the teacher says to him, "[meet me] first at such-and-such place." But the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Ezekiel (Ezekiel 3:22), "arise, go out to the valley," and when Ezekiel went out, he found the Holy One, blessed be He, had preceded him, as it is said (ibid. 3:23), "and I went out to the valley, and behold, the glory of the LORD stood there" — hence, "and Your humility has made me great."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:5: Luliani bar Savrei said in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak: see the humility that is in the Holy One, blessed be He — see what is written there (Exodus 19:19), "Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice" — it should only have said, "God spoke and Moses answered Him with a voice" — hence, "and Your humility has made me great."
